Bury St Edmunds
ber'ry saynt ed'mundz
n. (abbey town of Suffolk; where two men were hanged in 1583 for distributing Robert Browne's separatist books)
From Old English byrig, a fortified place, with the name of Edmund, the East Anglian king buried there.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Bury St Edmunds held one of the greatest English abbeys and, after its dissolution, one of the sharpest tests of the Elizabethan settlement. Robert Browne, the first Englishman to argue in print for churches gathered by voluntary covenant and independent of the bishops, had his books circulated in Suffolk; at the Bury assizes in June 1583 two men, John Copping and Elias Thacker, were tried for distributing them and hanged, their copies burnt before them. Browne himself was repeatedly imprisoned and eventually conformed. The monk Richard Bayfield, burnt in 1531 for importing Tyndale's books, had been of the abbey here. The dictionary records the town because the question Browne raised is a real one and the answer Gamaliel gave is the right procedure: “Refrain from these men, and let them alone: for if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought” (Act 5:38).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a separatist as one who withdraws from an established church; to assemble as to come together, to meet; and to overthrow as to demolish, to defeat, to destroy.

expand to see more

SEPARATIST, n. One that withdraws from a church, or rather from an established church, to which he has belonged; a dissenter.

ASSEMBLE, v.i. To meet or come together; to convene, as a number of individuals.

OVERTHROW, v.t. To turn upside down; to demolish; to destroy; to defeat; to conquer.

COVENANT, n. [L. convenio.] A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract.

Key Scripture

Act 5:38 — "And now I say unto you, Refrain from these men, and let them alone: for if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought:"

Act 5:39 — "But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God."

Mat 15:13 — "But he answered and said, Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up."

Heb 10:25 — "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching."

Modern Corruption

Two men hanged at the Bury assizes in June 1583 for distributing Robert Browne's separatist books, and their copies burnt before them.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the hanging. Whatever the merits of Browne's ecclesiology, two men died for carrying books in a Protestant kingdom, which is the same principle Mary's bishops used and the dictionary rejects in both hands. On the doctrine itself the dictionary is not neutral: it holds the congregational governance of the local church, which is Browne's substantial point, while rejecting the separatist temper that unchurches every assembly but its own and makes the purity of the gathered company a condition of Christ's presence in it.

The principle to recover is that God's work cannot be put down and men's work needs no persecuting. Gamaliel completes the argument: “But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it” (Act 5:39), lest you be found fighting against God. Christ says the same of every false growth, that “Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up” (Mat 15:13), and no magistrate is needed for the rooting. Meanwhile the duty of the believer is positive and unchanged: “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25).
